1. **Chart type**: Slope chart (two-point line chart comparing values between 2023 and 2050).

2. **Layout techniques**:
- Uses a **two-column comparison layout** with endpoints for **2023** and **2050**.
- Multiple regional series are shown as **parallel slope lines**.
- No faceting or stacking.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (2023, 2050) | Temporal | Horizontal position in two columns; column headers |
| Share of global population aged 15 to 24 (%) | Quantitative | Vertical position; numeric labels at endpoints |
| Region | Categorical/nominal | Separate line series; color/hue; text labels |
| Highlighted region status (Africa vs. others) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue emphasis (blue for Africa, orange for other regions) |

I live in North America, and It is certainly concerning to see that we are predicted to see less people in the upcoming young generations than we do now. It makes me think about American and Canadian cultures as well as birth rates.

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the distribution of young people (aged 15-24) now and how that is projected to change in the next 27 years. I notice that by 2050, Africa is projected to have the highest percentage of young people (35%). In human geography, we discussed how many countries of Africa have expansive population pyramids which means their population is young and growing. This is because most of these countries are developing countries which means they have not achieved a significant degree of industrialization relative to their populations, and have, in most cases, a medium to low standard of living. They lack access to education, especially for women, and they lack access to contraceptives/family planning. Therefore, women are getting married very young and having many kids. Additionally, having children in countries like Africa can be helpful because they can work for the family. On the other hand, I noticed that in 2050 Northern America will have the lowest percentage of young people (3.5%). This is most likely because of the cost of having children in the developed countries of North America. Since it costs so much, people are going to stop having as many children because they cannot afford it. Finally, I noticed that Eastern and Southeastern Asia suffered a dramatic decline in young people between the years 2023 and 2050. This is because countries like China and Japan have an aging population. Especially with China's one-child rule, the younger population will shrink. PT.2

comments.raw_comment:
From the graph, I noticed that in 2050 Africa will consist of the highest global population aged 15 to 24 at 35%. Africa is the only continent listed where the percentage of the age group in the population will increase (in 2023, Africa possesses 23% of the global population of 15 to 24). On the other hand, other continents and areas of the world will decrease in 2050 from obtaining their current population of 15 to 24 year-olds. This includes Southern Asia (with the highest 15-24 age population in 2030), Eastern and Southeastern Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, Europe, Western Asia, and North America. Therefore, Africa will experience a rise in young populations in the coming decades. I wonder how countries will respond to the following data. Particularly in North and South Korea, China and Japan, the population continues to significantly shrink which will cause significant issues concerning the future of the nations. This is also demonstrated in the graph as the steepest decline in the global population of 15 to 24 year olds from 24% in 2023, to 17% in 2050 by Eastern and Southeastern Asia. This relates to the world community as it relates to birth rates and the position of nations in the future. With the lack of a young population, countries will have a difficult time developing and rely more heavily on caring for the elderly. 

“Don’t Grow Up: A Decline in Young Populations Is a Danger for Future Nations”

comments.raw_comment: There is a sizeable increase in population for Africa, a historically underdeveloped continent as its general population lack many essentials like quantitative water resources, long-term housing solutions, and stable economic and social growth. The government in Africa has been corrupt in many, if not all, recognized countries within the continent, making it easy to stay away from them for immigration purposes. The increase in the youth population is more than likely because of the health conditions on each continent. As seen per the graph, Asia overall takes the largest dive in population growth, contributed mainly by the fact that Asia has the worst air quality and a significantly low birth rate. Struggling with pollution and a significant lack of resources, Asia seems to be the only continent steadily declining in its living environment as a desirable living place. With pollution kept in mind, Africa is by far the least industrialized continent in the world. As overpopulation ensues, Africa will make for a great alternative as it makes up ~20% of the world's land mass, meaning there is plenty of space for immigration and development, as it has generally gone unused.

Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “As The Rest Of The World Ages, Africa Is Becoming Younger” by Emily of Perth Amboy High School in N.J. and “Africa’s Future is Younger than the Rest” by Bailey of Iowa.
 
Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article that included this graph, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.

The next graphs will be released by Friday, April 11 with live-moderation on Wednesday, April 17.  The topic – global carbon-free electricity sources.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who believes that immigrants, like her students, are the source of more youth in the United States, and Bill Gottschalk of Collinsville, Illinois, who is excited to see how the youth of the future will transform powerful changes globally.

In this graph, I noticed that Africa has the highest predicted growth in the share of the global population in young adults and it is expected for them to have the largest share by 2050. The rest of the world is either expected to decline or be stagnant, with south and eastern Asia declining sharply compared to other parts of the world. 

I’m curious about how development and the costs of raising children have impacted these statistics. I am also curious about if  Africa is expected to have the highest share of young people because of the declining birth rates in other countries, because Africa is expected to have extraordinary growth in birth rates, or a combination of the two. 

This affects me and my community because it’s a matter that affects world politics. Africa becoming one of the regions with the most young people will naturally bring development to the region's economy and it may cause some companies to shift their factories and productions from Asia to a more young work-ready Africa. 

Africa Is to Become The Youngest Population In The World!

comments.raw_comment: Africa is expected to experience a 12% increase in population over the next 25 years, while Western Asia is projected to grow by only 0.4%. In contrast, the rest of the world is predicted to have a slight decline in population. This growth presents both advantages and difficulties. On one hand, it fosters greater diversity within the population. Moreover, the stability of other regions indicates societal stability and less need for extensive future planning due to resource loss. However, Africa encounters challenges like overcrowding and a severe lack of resources. The inadequate infrastructure in Africa raises concerns about sustaining the expanding population, potentially leading to starvation and higher mortality rates. Additionally, the population surge may result in a decrease in job availability, with certain sectors becoming oversaturated. This could lead to lower wages and an increase in homelessness. Observing the data, I questioned Africa's ability to manage this substantial population growth. The graph is relevant to the global community as it demonstrates the projected population shifts in the coming years. A fitting title for this graph could be "Population Growth: Is Your Region Ready for the Future?" By selecting an inclusive title, readers can relate the graph to their own area and contemplate the potential consequences of population growth.

I notice that almost all nations with more than 1% of the global population will see a decrease in their share of people aged 15 to 24 between 2023 and 2050, indicating an aging population. Both developed regions (such as Europe) and less developed regions (such as Latin America and the Caribbean) are experiencing this trend. Eastern and Southeastern Asia will have the largest drop-- from 24% to 17%. Interestingly, 15 to 24 years olds will increase in Africa (23% to 35%) and Western Asia (4% to 4.4%).

I wonder if Eastern Asia will have a smaller younger population because of the effects of One Child Policy. I also wonder if Africa will have more young people due to increased access to healthcare, which would limit infant mortality. Lastly, I am curious if countries' share of the global population aged 15 to 24 is indicative of future population size? Will those with a higher a younger population experience more growth?

This effects me and my community because the redistribution of young people will have influence the demographics of my country. As an American, the 0.5% decrease between 2023 and 2050 may seem small, but may suggest an aging population.

"Kids These Days: Changing Global Demographics"

comments.raw_comment:
3/27/2024

	This graph reflects the percentage of the world’s youth, that is people between the ages of 15 and 24, which is predicted to belong to each of a number of distinct geographical regions by 2050. The graph suggests that 35% of the world’s youth will reside in Africa, which seems to coincide with that continent’s broader development as many countries there begin to transform into modern societies. It seems important to note that this graph, however, seems misleading. The implication it delivers is that Africa will experience a population boom of sorts and so its youth population will rise dramatically. This may well be true; however, if one considers that Africa is an entire continent comprising more than 20% of the Earth’s total landmass, the context of this number changes. Indeed, while the graph’s constructors have split up Asia into three separate regions, when one combines these numbers, it becomes evident that the Asian continent will contain 47.4% of the world’s youth population in 2050, the lion’s share. This data is, for whatever reason, hidden in the graph. It seems, furthermore, nonsensical to consider what percentage of the world’s youth such massive continents will hold as it renders the data shallow, as well as reinforcing misguided conceptions of these continents as singular places instead of diverse regions. One cannot, therefore, examine much from this data.

I notice that Africa is predicted to have the highest share (35%) of the global population aged 15-24. This is an increase of 12% in 27 years. I also notice that Eastern and Southeastern Asia are predicted to have a share of 17% of the global population aged 15 to 24. This is a decrease of 7% in 27 years. I wonder why Africa will hold such a great share of the global population aged 15-24. I did some research and found that Niger has the highest birth rate in the world. I found out that this is a country within Africa and I can conclude that this most definitely impacted this statistic and is the reason why it is predicted to increase. I wonder if the reason that the percentage has decreased in Eastern and Southeastern Asia is partly a product of China’s one-child policy that existed for 36 years, one that completely stunted their population growth. I know that in 2020 the average number of babies a woman has in her lifetime was well below the 2.1 needed to keep a population stable. I wonder how this decline in youth and population will affect the country’s economy in the years to come. This relates to the world community as population rates have a direct effect on the economy, politics, and overall quality of life.

Population Panic
